utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Call the case, please, Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning. Case number IT-02-60-T, the Prosecutor versus Vidoje Blagojevic and Dragan Jokic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Good morning, ladies and gentlemen. Since we have the Plenary Session on Thursday, it is our intention to finish the two witnesses in three days. If we cannot make it, we have to find some time on Friday. Good morning, Witness. Can you hear me?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can hear you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Would you please stand up and take the solemn declaration, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. You may sit down, please. Well, Mr. McCloskey, are you ready?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. You may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: First if I could hand this to the usher, and Mr. Witness, if you could take a look at that name and just firm for confirm for us if that is in fact you, without saying your name.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P105
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you. And can you tell us, are you Muslim by faith?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P105
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And what opstina were you born in?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P105
utterances.text: Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: What year?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P105
utterances.text: The 18th of October, 1937.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And did you live most of your life in Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P105
utterances.text: Yes, I did. I was born there. That's where I lived. Both my father and my grandfather were born there and lived there. And occasionally I went out of there to work, but I never went abroad anywhere.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: What did you do for a living?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P105
utterances.text: I worked on my land as a farmer. I had my gardens. I had cattle. Or I was also earning money as a bricklayer.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And were you living in Srebrenica in July 1995?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P105
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And what did you and your family do on 11 July 1995?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P105
utterances.text: On the 11th of July, that's when there was shelling in Srebrenica, and we gathered our things together in a bag and we just went in the direction of Potocari, towards UNPROFOR, together with the rest of the people, as we were fleeing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Could I interrupt, Mr. McCloskey? Would you please inform us about this witness's pseudonym, just for the sake of the record.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes. It's P105.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And why did you want your family and yourself to flee your home in Srebrenica to go to Potocari?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P105
utterances.text: Because we tried to save our lives. We wanted to set off towards Tuzla to get to the free territory. Apart from that, we didn't think that -- it didn't happen as we thought it would. We got to Potocari. There was a mass of people there, well over 25, 30.000 people. What do I know? There were four factories of people. Not all the people could get into factory halls. People were lying in the streets. It was completely packed with people. Everyone was fleeing to save their lives.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And what family members went with you to Potocari?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P105
utterances.text: My daughter, my wife, four grandchildren, and my daughter-in-law, with those children.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: These grandchildren, were they young, from about ages 1 through maybe 10?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P105
utterances.text: Something like that. From about a year, year and a half, up to 10, yes. Four of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And did you have two adult sons at that time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P105
utterances.text: Yes. I had two sons, and they set off. One of them went towards the hospital to get the wounded out and to load them onto a lorry to see them off to Bratunac, and when they took the wounded out, put them onto that lorry, he then set off towards the woods. Both of them set off towards the woods, together with the army. There were soldiers, as well as civilians, and they set off together. But they couldn't get through, so somewhere along that road they were stopped, captured, killed. I buried one son on Friday in Potocari, and the other was not found.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: About what time did your family arrive in Potocari on the 11th?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P105
utterances.text: We arrived sometime about 2.00 or 3.00 in the afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And where did you spend the night that first night on the 11th in Potocari?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P105
utterances.text: Well, I spent the night outside, because the factory halls were full. There were five or six factories there. But they were all full of people. So I was in the street, and there were many other people in the street.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Did you --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P105
utterances.text: And on the roads.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Did your family have any food and water with you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P105
utterances.text: We brought water from there. There were some pumps. There was a little bit of food, just a little bit of food, and that's how we spent the night.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: On the morning of the 12th, can you tell us what you recall happening on the 12th of July.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P105
utterances.text: On the 12th of July, that's when a man came with a kind of trumpet and he spoke on a microphone, said what his name was, that nobody should be afraid, that the Serb army would come there, that there would be negotiations, that they would be walking among the people, just to see for a while if no one was armed with guns or pistols or knives. And that day, soldiers arrived. They started walking among the people. They walked through the people on that day. Mladic also came. And there was a small lorry that came and they brought the bread and they threw the bread loaves onto the people. And the people were catching the bread loaves. And I thought that was good. And as they were throwing the bread, I managed to get one loaf. And as this was being done, they were filming it to show the world how humane and good they were. But when they were committing the genocide, then they weren't filming at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Was this enough bread for these thousands of people?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P105
utterances.text: It wasn't enough. It was just brought, I think, so that it can be filmed and shown.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Where did you stay most of the day on the 12th of July?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P105
utterances.text: Well, I spent -- outside again, and I saw about eight or nine dogs. They were Alsatians, large dogs, with soldiers. They were walking among the people, the people that were there that day. And that night, when that night fell, then horrible things started to happen. There was a scream of a woman. There would be a scream and then everybody would jump up if they heard that. And after a while, you would hear people screaming, crying for help. And occasionally would hear a shot or not. Then there would be a noise and then the noise would die down. So what they did, what they killed people with, we don't know. Occasionally we heard gunshots, occasionally we didn't. That was horrible. In the night I saw two soldiers. When they started going among the people, one of his arms was bleeding, about here, and he came among the women and said: Have you got any water to wash my arm? One woman asked: What happened to you? And he said: I got knocked. So that's how -- and then he went off. That woman had no water. That was happening all night. So of course we couldn't sleep enough. Everybody was upset. There was noise. We could hear what was going on. We were in fear. And that night, we spent it in this way. And many of them were brought out and they died in the night.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Did you actually see anyone abused in any way or did you just hear it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P105
utterances.text: I heard that. I heard screams, screams of the people outside. And the shots. I heard that. I didn't see it with my own eyes, but I heard it with my own ears. And I heard it said by other people, but I didn't see it with my own eyes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Now, on the 13th of July, in the morning, can you tell us what you and your family did, the next day.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P105
utterances.text: The next morning when I got up, we thought we just want to get onto the buses so that we wouldn't be there, but there were so many people. There were so many people, I couldn't get through. From the morning to about 1.00 to 2.00 in the afternoon, I somehow managed to get to the bus. And when I got down there, there was a barricade set up by the Serb army. They were letting about 150 people, as much as they could, go on to the onto buses. I then went past this barricade. About 15 metres away, there was a second barricade. This is where they were separating men from the women and children.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Who was with you when you made it to this second barricade?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P105
utterances.text: Four grandchildren and my daughter-in-law. My wife had fainted, and she was with my daughter, with UNPROFOR, trying to get some medical assistance. And then I was separated, and the children went by themselves to the bus, with the daughter-in-law. I was carrying the water in a cannister for me and for the children, but since I was separated, I just gave my grandson the cannister, and I had to return. I was taken to a house where there were more men who had been separated. And then again more men came, and when that house got completely full, then two buses came.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Let me ask you: Can you describe the person or persons that separated you at this barricade, what they were wearing, what they looked like.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P105
utterances.text: Well, I can describe that they were wearing multicoloured uniforms, Serb uniforms. They were multicoloured.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Did you see any other men separated from their families at this time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P105
utterances.text: Yes, because in the house where I had been separated to, then they separated more men and more men came to that house, and that's how the house got full. There was even an upstairs and a basement. We were then told, and the women, see, we are just -- we just want to ask you some questions and then you'll be released. They were saying one thing, but they were doing another.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: While you were in this house, did any Serb soldier take your name?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P105
utterances.text: I only saw one soldier who came to the door and said: Has anybody got Deutschmarks? And one of them said: I have a hundred Deutschmarks. And then he said: Quickly, give me, give me that, before another one comes. So that man came -- gave him 100 Deutschmarks and the soldier left. But there was no mistreatment in that house. I didn't see any.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: While you were in that house, did anyone interview you or take your name?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P105
utterances.text: Nobody asked me my name.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And how long were you in that house until the vehicles came and took you away from there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P105
utterances.text: Well, perhaps about half an hour, maybe an hour. I don't know. Half an hour, perhaps. And then two buses came and then we got onto the buses, sat down, and we were off to Bratunac.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Were there any soldiers on your bus?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P105
utterances.text: There were always soldiers, perhaps one, sometimes two, escorting the camp prisoners, so that nobody would protest. There was always one or two Serb soldiers. We got to Bratunac, and there we got to the school, Vuk Karadzic. That is the name of the school. And we got to the school, we all had to leave our bags, if we had any, and take the food with us. But we had to leave the bags outside. That's what was ordered and that's what we did. So we went in there. We sat down. It was very dusty. That school had been half destroyed. It was old, and that's where we sat down, and a large group came. And then we had to move to upstairs. That's where we spent the night. And then that's when mistreatment, torture, started. There was a --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Before we get to that, the night, let me ask you a couple of other questions. About --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P105
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: About what time of day did you arrive at this school in Bratunac?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P105
utterances.text: Well, perhaps we arrived in the afternoon, about 2.00 or 3.00 in the afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: You've described the school as old. Was it known as "the old school"?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P105
utterances.text: No, but what I mean is it was dilapidated. That's why I said "old." But its name was Vuk Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yesterday in my office, did you have a chance to look at a map of Bratunac and mark a school on that map?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P105
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I've got that map here. It's P57. If we could place it on the ELMO, and I'd just ask the witness to see if he recognises this map.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. I don't see the -- is the ELMO working? There we go.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P105
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Well, can you just look at this map yourself, then? It's next to you. Okay. I see it now. If you could look -- sir, look at the map that's next to you. Don't look at your screen.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P105
utterances.text: Next to me? What do you mean?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: If you could take a look at the actual map, and could you point to the --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P105
utterances.text: Here it is. Here it is. Ljubovija, Sase. These are the roads leading to it. Here it is to Sase. This if from Potocari, and here, towards this crossroads here in this direction, there's the school, Vuk Karadzic, where we were, this one here. Now, I'm not certain 100 per cent --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: -- On the ELMO. Okay. Thank you. Okay. The school you're pointing to with the pointer, could you do that again.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P105
utterances.text: [Indicates]

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And you've actually circled that school on that map, haven't you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P105
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And those are your initials right next to the school?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P105
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. And you were telling us about how sure you were about this. Can you tell us that? And we don't need the map any more, Mr. Witness. How sure are you that that was the place where you were -- you stayed in Bratunac?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P105
utterances.text: I'm 90 per cent sure, since there were two other buildings, large buildings, there. So I'm 90 per cent sure that that's the one, the one that I indicated. I'm 90 per cent sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: How many nights did you stay in Bratunac?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P105
utterances.text: I spent two nights there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And where did you spend those two nights?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P105
utterances.text: We spent those nights in the school, and when we arrived at the school, they immediately arrived and started maltreating us, and we saw that there was no goodness. We realised there was no goodness. And then a policeman arrived in a blue uniform. He had a white belt, a pistol, a holster, and he started beating someone right in front of us. He beat him with an automatic rifle. He beat him around the head and the shoulders. He then bowed his head, and the policeman took the rifle in order to put his head back into position, and made a gesture like this. He then got hold of some sort of rubber implement. He took that implement and hit him twice, and then he took the automatic rifle, and then with both his hands, from above, hit him in the head, and the man was covered in blood. The man's face was covered in blood. And his shirt was covered in blood too. And then the policeman, who got angry, beat him. He then left. But this man was covered in blood. He remained sitting there. Then he came to where our group was in the room and sat there for about half an hour among us, after having been beaten with this rubber whip, and then this man appeared at the door again and called to him. He didn't want to get up. He knew that the situation was dangerous. This person, this policeman, shouted at him. He had to go out. Then shouts, screams could be heard. I can describe everything to you, but I can't describe the sounds that we heard. He made various sounds as he was screaming and he never returned again. And this happened on several occasions. They took people out, day and night.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Now, can you describe what the people that took people out were wearing, about how many different people were involved in taking people out, and what were they wearing?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P105
utterances.text: Well, there were soldiers in camouflage uniforms, Serbian soldiers in camouflage uniforms, and there were also men in blue uniforms, police uniforms. So they took people out and day and night you could hear people groaning outside. And if I had a look out of the window, there would be a burst of fire and you would have to crouch down. You wouldn't be able to look out of the window.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So were you ever able to see anything outside during those two days you were there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P105
utterances.text: No, I didn't see the road, not even the road, because I wasn't able to approach the window. I preferred to remain in peace rather than to try and look out. But even if I could have looked out of the window, it was -- it would have been difficult for me to do so because of the fear I felt and the sadness I felt.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: How many people were in this upstairs room that you were taken to?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P105
utterances.text: Well, perhaps about 200 people, because that room was a big room. But they were all crammed into that room. That's as far as that room is concerned. But I don't know how many people there were in other rooms, because we weren't allowed to move around. Lives were at stake. And then we saw that things did not bode well for us.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Could you tell if there were other people in other rooms in this school?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P105
utterances.text: Well, there were -- I know that because I heard their voices. I heard them walking around and so on. Perhaps someone would go to the toilet and then you would hear them going to the toilet or you would hear the soldiers approaching the door or approaching our door and singling out the persons they wanted to single out and taking them away. Quite a few people died in Bratunac, were killed in Bratunac, at the beginning of the war, when Arkan's men approached. Lots of people from Bratunac were arrested and detained at the playground. There were many neighbours of mine who were there, who had been captured. And those that had been captured, out of those that had been captured, a group was exchanged, went to Sarajevo, Tuzla, I don't know where.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Let's try to stay with 1995, if we can, Mr. Witness.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P105
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: For the roughly two nights that you spent at that school, can you give any -- an estimate of how many men were taken out that didn't come back, how many Muslim men were taken out and didn't come back?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P105
utterances.text: It's difficult for me to say. All I know is that people were taken out, and I know that there was a lot of groaning and screaming outside, day and night, non-stop. They must have been doing this in shifts. It could not have been just one shift responsible for this, since this happened day and night. You could hear this constantly. They were taking them out, one person at a time or two at a time. I saw them being taken out. I couldn't look out of the window because I was afraid, and there was shooting there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Did you notice a shift change, different soldiers or policemen replacing others that were guarding you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P105
utterances.text: I didn't, because I didn't know them. For a while, a person would be present and for a while he would be absent. I didn't know those soldiers, those policemen. Some would appear, others would appear and visit and torture people. I don't know how they acted. But given all the screaming and groaning, genocide was being committed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: After the second night and the next -- the day after the second night, the day you left, can you describe that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P105
utterances.text: Yes, I can describe it. Buses would arrive, going towards Tuzla. There were some buses. We got out, sat in them, and in the buses they told us that we weren't allowed to look to the left or right. We were just told to remain sitting and to keep our heads down, and that's how we travelled. There were seven buses. That's something that a friend of mine told me. He counted them. When we got to Konjevic Polje, they didn't head towards Vlasenica. They headed towards Zvornik.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Let me stop you for a moment. During your two days in the school in Bratunac, were you given any food by your captors?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P105
utterances.text: We weren't given anything, only water. But as far as food is concerned, we would receive a slice of bread when we sat down in the buses. They gave us this bread in the buses, and some sort of a biscuit or juice. I wasn't even able to eat this. I put it in my mouth and chewed it for about 15 minutes, but it was impossible to eat it. So we didn't have much food and there wasn't enough water. That's when we were given a little food and we weren't given food after that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: How thirsty --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P105
utterances.text: After the second or third day.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: How thirsty were you in that school in Bratunac? Did they give you enough water?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P105
utterances.text: There wasn't enough water. There was water, but not enough. For however much they would bring, we drank it all. I never felt that thirsty. However much you would drink, you would sweat it all out, because we were afraid or hungry. I don't know why it was like this, but we were very thirsty.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Did they treat anyone, give any medical aid to anyone during those two days you spent in that school in Bratunac?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P105
utterances.text: No, no one. How they treat anyone, they didn't care whether people would live or die, why would they treat anyone, even if there were sick people? That's how it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Now, you've described you're on a bus and you're heading towards Zvornik. Were there any soldiers or police on your bus?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P105
utterances.text: Yes. I know there were sometimes two soldiers in each bus, sometimes one soldier in each bus. They were escorting these buses to prevent people from fleeing. But usually there were two soldiers in each bus. When we got into the buses and arrived in Konjevic Polje, we headed towards Zvornik, not towards Tuzla. We arrived in Zvornik, and when we arrived there, we crossed a bridge over the Drina, got into Serbia, and then arrived as far as Loznica. And then returned to Bosnia, crossed a bridge again, and towards Pilica. When we arrived in Pilica, I don't know whether it was near Pilica, the buses stopped there and remained there for a while. Perhaps they were waiting for night to fall. There was a big building to the right. Perhaps they wanted a camp in that school and then realised that it wasn't possible because it was full. I don't know. But we waited there for an hour, an hour and a half, and then they shouted out to us in the bus and they said: There's someone lying down. Get him up. Make him stand up. Two people tried to get him up and then they said: He's dead. He's died. They said: Take him out by the road. Which is what they did. And then one of the persons who had taken him out asked the Serbian soldier, he said: Can I relieve myself outside? He went out, and then there were two bursts of fire, and someone said: Look, they've killed him. He fell down. He wanted to run away. He preferred trying to run away and being killed by a bullet rather than being the victim of genocide. He knew he would be killed by a bullet. And that's where we were, and then when night had fallen, the buses left.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Excuse me. Did you actually see that man get shot or did people just tell you that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P105
utterances.text: I heard the bursts of fire, but someone else told me that they had killed him. Another person saw him being killed and told me about it. I was near that person. But I didn't see the victim fall. I was told that he had been killed. There were two bursts of fire.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Did you see that victim run away, though?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P105
utterances.text: I saw him when he got out, and when he approached some sort of bushes, but this acquaintance of mine saw him falling near a bush.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Did you actually see this dead man on the bus that was taken and just thrown off the bus?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P105
utterances.text: I saw them getting him up and saying that he was dead, and I heard them saying that he should be taken out. I was in the bus myself. I saw that person. I saw them taking him out and leaving him by the road.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Did you know his name?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P105
utterances.text: No, I didn't. No one told me his name. I didn't know the person.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Now, did you recognise you were in Pilica from your own knowledge or did someone tell you that that was Pilica?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P105
utterances.text: I didn't know it was Pilica at the time. I had never been there in peacetime either. But later on I asked someone, who had a look at a map and told me that it was Pilica. Later on I asked other people too, and they also told me it was Pilica. Several people confirmed this. It's near Bijeljina. That's where Pilica is. From Zvornik towards Bijeljina.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Where did you -- the bus go after the incidents you've described in Pilica?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P105
utterances.text: The buses left, perhaps an hour and a half later. It was dark. We travelled for a while and then turned left. There was a school that they took us to. They took us up to the floor. We were crammed into a room on that floor, and again they started coming, taking people out, beating people, and you would hear groaning again, screaming, just like in Bratunac, day and night. They entered the room several times, the room I was in, and they took people out. And I don't know how many people there were in the other rooms, but my room, the room I was in, was crammed, full of people. They took people out. You could hear constant groaning, day and night. And we spent one night in this way, and then the second night they would bring a little water in. There was no bread, no food. We were hungry. But we had water to drink. It was very hot.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Are you sure you spent two nights in Pilica, at the Pilica school -- excuse me - at this school that you've described?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P105
utterances.text: One night or two nights, but as far as I know, we spent two nights there. One person said: Is there anything for us to eat? And the soldier said: We haven't got anything. We haven't got anything for ourselves either. And maybe half an hour later, he brought in a piece of bread, broke it up, and threw it to the people. Some people would get hold of a little bit of bread, eat it, but there was not much. It was a form of maltreatment, and that's how it was. And on the last day there were seven or eight men I knew in that room, but I wasn't able to enter the other rooms. If you wanted to go to the toilet, you would have to ask a soldier, and sometimes he would let you, sometimes he wouldn't. Sometimes he would say you have to wait. You would then have to wait for half an hour. Then the soldiers would arrive and line up in the corridor, and then there would be a column of us heading towards the toilet. Some would be beaten with a butt of a rifle while going to the toilet. But you had to go. That's how it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Were you given any water while you were at that school?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P105
utterances.text: Yes. We were given some water, but not enough, because too much water was drunk. Too much water was drunk. It was very hot, and people were afraid. It wasn't enough. There were many people who turned black, and even if you knew these people, it was difficult to recognise them; they had changed so much. Their bodies would be green. If we didn't have the little water that we did have, many people would have died of thirst and of fear.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Could you describe what happened the day you left that school.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P105
utterances.text: Children were lined up. They said: How many boys are there, from 14 to 15 or 16 years of age? And about 12 came forward and lined up, and they said: Avdic needs such boys. You'll go and see Avdic. The children smiled a bit. You know, they seemed to be happy. They took them to the other rooms. They took them out of these rooms, the other rooms. I don't know how many children there were in the other rooms, but they took these children out of my room. I don't know what happened. I don't know what they did to them. I don't know whether they went to Avdic. I don't know whether they were killed or whether they were taken to camps. I know nothing about this. I didn't see where they were taken. And later they said: Whoever has money can go to Sarajevo. The ticket to Sarajevo is 20 German marks. Some people said that they had the money. One person said he had a hundred marks. He said: I can pay for myself and for four relatives, or friends of mine. He said he could pay for five people. And they left in groups like this. Perhaps there was a bus or two buses. They paid and left. The buses returned quickly. And then we were told even if people don't have money, they can leave. There were two canvases. They said: Tear this up. And they gave two of us this canvas and said: Tear it up and tie the hands behind their backs. They tied them up and then people left in groups. But the buses left rapidly and then returned. They said: You've got to go to Tuzla. But the buses would return very quickly. If I'm going to Tuzla, going to be free, why would they tie me up? But they were tying people up, and this was suspicious, in my opinion. So I thought, it's my turn. I had my hands tied up, and then as we were leaving, at the bottom of the stairs, when I reached the basement, there was concrete down there. A man had been killed there. Blood was running out of his head. He was bleeding. He was lying there on the concrete. We were in a column with hands tied behind our backs, heading in the direction of the buses. We reached the buses. These Serbian soldiers were swearing and shouting at us. They would occasionally hit someone with the butt of their rifles. I got to the bus. As far as I can remember, there was a company called the 7th of July. We sat down there. I got to the bus. I looked in front of me, towards the shade, and there were some officers there, I think. They were talking to each other. They had automatic rifles. They didn't speak to us. They just observed us. They observed their soldiers swearing at us, hitting some of us. All they did was observe and smile to themselves, and they watched us getting into the buses, and they spoke among themselves. We got into the buses. They said the buses were going to Tuzla. When we left in those buses, after about 2, 2 and a half kilometres, I heard shooting on a hill. I heard a noise. When we arrived at the hill, the buses stopped. When they stopped, the doors opened. The Serbian soldiers surrounded the buses. They cursed us and they cursed Alija and Haris and then death appeared in front of you. As we got out, they stopped us. I remained in one half of the bus. Another column headed off down a path. There were some corpses, and that column headed in the direction of those corpses. They arrived at the field where the corpses were. I observed from the bus. There were two bursts of fire. Everyone fell down. They came again. I was in that other half of the bus. They cursed us and Alija and Haris. It was the same curse again. And they shouted. I got out. We were in a column, single file. Our hands were behind our backs. We bowed our heads and we proceeded like this. When a Serbian soldier was -- there was a Serbian soldier in front of me and another one behind me. There were about eight of us escorting us -- eight of them escorting us. They had automatic rifles, and one of them told me: Give me some German marks. I said I didn't have any. He kicked me in the stomach. I doubled over. I fell down and I got up. The second Serbian soldier said: Don't commit genocide. He said: Kill like a soldier if you want to kill. So I had to get up and go along with the column. And then the same man who had kicked me said: Does anyone want to cross over into Serbs? And two of them, two people, said they would. But nothing came of that. And as we were walking, somebody said: Give us water to drink and then kill us. And nothing came of that either. We arrived at where the corpses were, and then we walked through those groups of corpses at the end. And then there were those corpses and then there were more, and then it was quite a difficult terrain. And then they told us to stand straight and to turn our backs, so we did. And then they said: Lie down. But before they said "lie down," there was a burst of fire, and in that speed, I fell. Nothing hit me, but I fell. Another person fell on top of me. I knew him. And so I was lying down. Everybody fell down immediately, and so did I, as if I had been shot down. And there was a Serb soldier who shouted out after the fire had stopped: Is there anyone alive? And then somebody shouted out: I'm alive. And another person: I am alive, too. Kill me. And so this soldier went over there and possibly fired just one shot for each one, and that was that. I wasn't hit. And then after that, more buses were emptied, about six or seven columns were brought while I was lying there on the ground. And there were more and more people below me, and around me. There was firing above me. I would get dust on top of me, even rubble, as the shots were being fired. And after every single column was shot, they would execute -- they would ask: Is there anybody alive? Occasionally there would be one or two; occasionally there would be nobody. And that's how they brought six or seven columns. After they brought all them, killed them off, executed them, then they didn't bring any more buses. After a while, they left to where they had brought them from. There was a house. There was a garden. Perhaps that's where they stayed. During the day I thought for a while whether I could untie myself. I thought if I didn't shout out, they could just kill me. I managed to get my tie off. I was lying on my front and I managed to get the hand tie off my hands, and then I put them again on my back, because I knew that the patrol would come, so that they would see that I had my hands untied. That's why I put the hands on my back as if they were tied, so they wouldn't notice me. And then a patrol came. There were five of them. I was lying on my front. And I faced away from where they were coming. They arrived, five of them arrived. I saw them. They were walking among the dead. And then they shouted: Look, there's one running away. Look, there's another one running away. And then they would fire, fire, single shots, bursts of fire. They would be firing towards the fields where these two had run off. And there was one who -- some of them went off, and one of them stayed with the corpses. After about a quarter of an hour, two of them returned, and the one who had remained said: What happened? And then the two said: One of them escaped. He hid. Which meant that one of them they killed. But then they said: The other two had remained to look for him. Hopefully they will find him, they said. And then they said: We committed genocide just like in 1941 in Jasenovac. That's how they were talking among themselves. They were there for a while. And then they went off to the shade. They just went off. I then looked into the sky to see where the sun was, to see how much I had before dark. And I was trying to see where the woods were, because I was worried about the machines coming to dig those bodies. And to dig the earth to put the bodies in, and I was afraid of that. And I could see that there was two more hours, two and a half, until darkness fell. I could see that by the sky. And then I heard some whispering nearby. Somebody said: Is there somebody alive? Let's get out. And then I started to take the ties off my hands to prepare myself to flee. And as I got the tie off my hands, I saw there were two of them going into some bushes down in the field. There was some grass. There was a hundred, 150 square metres in that area, and I thought I should go that way too. So I took the ties off my hands. The other two managed to get into the bushes where I thought I'd go as well. I jumped up to my legs. I couldn't crouch for a long time, couldn't crawl, because I was worried about a patrol coming. So I thought I would just jump. I ran across corpse, dead bodies, from one dead body to another. There was no soil. I stepped on, and the corpses were moving as I walked on them. I was looking at them, and listening out for somebody shouting: Look, there's one escaping. Because I was worried about that. And then I got to the bush. I crouched down. Nobody shouted anything out. And then I looked around me, and then I saw two more people coming out into the bushes. When they got into the bushes -- so there were five of us there, and there was nobody else. Everybody else was dead.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Witness, let me ask you just a couple of questions, if I could.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P105
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: On the bus trip from the school to the execution fields, were there any soldiers on your bus?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P105
utterances.text: From the school, yes, there were. There were. By the school, there was a group that only directed people to get to the buses. And then one or two soldiers would board the buses to escort them to the execution site. And there was another group that waited up there at the site, met the people, and killed them. That was their organisation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And at that killing field, did you ever have a chance to view the whole field to get some kind of an estimate of how many people lay dead there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P105
utterances.text: Well, as far as dead bodies are concerned, I'm certain there were about a thousand and a thousand and a half. I guarantee this, because as soon as I jumped to my feet, the first thing I did was to turn around and look around me. And when I got off from there into the darkness, got out of the bush, on the other side -- there were corpses on the other side. But I didn't know they were there until I got there. A thousand to a thousand and a half, certainly. In that speed, I managed to see this. There were many corpses, many dead. Many dead lay down.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: We know that over the next several days you were escaping from various Serbs and you met some Muslims and other things, but I want to just ask you about the day you decided to surrender. So if we could go directly to that day. Can you tell us about how many days after the executions you decided to surrender.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P105
utterances.text: Well, I can say that it was like this: It was possibly that it was on the 17th of July that the execution took place, 16th or the 17th, and it was on the 26th that I surrendered. That's when the Red Cross registered me. I have that very clear in my mind. 26th. So it was from the 17th to the 26th that I was on the run. And then I surrendered on the 26th, and that's when I was registered, on that day.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: What kind of forces did you surrender to, or what kind of authorities?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P105
utterances.text: I surrendered when I arrived. There was a civilian, and then they told me: Go to the bus. So I went there. But the police was there. There were two policemen and a driver. And that's where I surrendered. They drove us around, drove us around, and they came in front of a bar. And they stopped the bus and they went off to the bar to get the cigarettes. And I saw they were drinking beer outside the bar. And then the waiter found out who else was on the bus, and I saw him going to the bar. And he carried out two packs of cigarettes and a 2-litre pack of juice, and he brought it to the bus, and the police came. And he said: There's the cigarettes. There's some juice for you to drink. Freshen up and cheer up. I, like everyone, he said, I've been working in Germany for 22 years, and I'm on good terms with everyone. And he said: Are you hungry? And I said: Of course I'm hungry, for a fortnight I haven't seen a piece of bread. Of course I would like to eat. Because I had just been eating fruit in the forest. Things were quite bitter and sour. And he said: Well, come in front of the bar. Have something to eat. So he gave us lunch and meat. As far as I remember, there was meat and there was potatoes. So we ate well. The other man couldn't each very much. He felt sick.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Were you with another person at that time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P105
utterances.text: Yes, I was with another survivor. There were two of us. So we were sitting there. We had a cup of coffee. I thanked him later. I didn't dare ask about his name, because I was afraid. But this is something beautiful to me. The nice words he spoke to me and what he gave me. That was as if he had built me a house. It was a big thing that he did for me, very kind. I can't forget that. If everyone had been like this, there would have been no war. One man can be worth a thousand men, and one man can destroy everyone if he's evil.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: This waiter was a Serb?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P105
utterances.text: He was a Serb. He was in their area, and he was a Serb. But when a man is kind, it doesn't matter whether he's a Muslim or a Serb, or whatever faith he is. That's not important. It's important that he was a good man. He was a Serb, and I respect him as a real man, and I'll never forget that. Really, it's as if he gave me a whole house and not just a pack of cigarettes and juice.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: One last question. If you could try to describe for us the impact this crime has had on you and your family and your life.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P105
utterances.text: Well, the effect. What can I tell you? It couldn't have been any worse. While I had two sons, they were helping me, working on the farm, and then they escaped to serve their heads. And then somebody just came and killed all those innocent people. Who didn't intend to harm anything or anyone. And whatever kind of genocide took place, this could only have been prevented by the Serb authorities. Nobody should have been killed. Nobody should have been killed. They could have prevented this and they could have also ordered for people to be executed. Those in authority, they could have ordered the kill and they could have saved everyone, what they wanted to do, that's what they did. And today, we don't have a good life and they don't have a good life either, but that's what they deserve. Nobody should be angry with anyone. Everyone makes good or bad things for themselves and to themselves.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. Well, Witness, we are going to have a break. Please remain where you are --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: -- for a while, and later on Madam Usher will show you out of the courtroom. But at this moment, please remain where you are. We'll resume at 10 minutes to 11.00.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. I understand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Any cross-examination? Mr. Karnavas.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: No cross-examination, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Stojanovic, any cross-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No cross-examination. No questions. I was told by my client that there should be no questions asked of this witness, with the sincere gratitude for him coming to testify today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. Well, it seems to me that the Judges have no questions to this witness. At this stage, are there any documents to tender, Mr. McCloskey?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. We have the one map, number 57, but that's it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Any objections, Mr. Karnavas?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: No objections, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Stojanovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No objections, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. This piece of evidence is admitted. Well -- yes, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. President. I'm reminded that we should have P58 as the piece of paper with his name on it, that should be part of the record also.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I believe that it will become a rule that whenever that piece of -- with his name on it should be admitted, without any tendering procedures. That is applied to both parties. Thank you, Witness, for coming here to give your evidence. This Trial Chamber would like to express great sympathy to you. All we wish is that you have good luck in the future.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Thank you, and thank you for those who assisted me in coming here to be at this trial, and thanks to those who have set up this Court to find the truth and justice. And I know that it is difficult for criminals when they threw 8.000 people into mass graves and more than 8.000. I know that they are sorry that they didn't throw me into a mass grave, but they couldn't throw me. One saved me, dear Allah saved me. I know that otherwise they would have wanted to erase me and everything else. And thank you, Your Honour. Thank you, everyone.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. When the usher pulls down the blinds, she will take you out of this courtroom. We wish you a pleasant journey back home.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. McCloskey, who is the next witness, or what's his pseudonym?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes. This next witness has a pseudonym, and it is 106.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And that is Mr. Waespi's witness, and so we'll take a moment and make a change. And we have three -- a total of three Bosnian witnesses, and if there's not much cross-examination, we should be able to get them all on before the plenary break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Good morning, Witness. Can you hear me? Good morning, Witness. Can you hear me?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Would you please take the solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Are we starting?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. You may sit down, please. Yes, Mr. Waespi.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. President. Good morning, Your Honours. Just before --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: -- the witness starts, I would like to inform you that the witness will be referring to two Prosecution exhibits, Prosecution Exhibit 10/1 and 10/3. He will not be referring to a map, Prosecution Exhibit 20.1, but I think it may assist Your Honours to follow the testimony of the witness. And again, if the witness could be shown a piece of paper.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And Witness, do you see a name written on that piece of paper?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P106
utterances.text: Yes, I can see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And without reading it, is that your name?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P106
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Good morning, Witness.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P106
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Are you feeling okay?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P106
utterances.text: Well, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I would like to ask you a few preliminary questions, and then we'll go into more detail about what happened in July 1995. Let me ask you first: Were you born in 1944?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P106
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And you're a Muslim by faith?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P106
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And in 1995, you were a member of the Bosnian army?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P106
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Now, let's go to July 1995. You were working as a farmer on your fields in your community, which is in the opstina of Srebrenica; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P106
utterances.text: That's right, yes. I was working the land.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Now, this community, is it very close to the town of Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P106
utterances.text: Very close by, 10, 12 kilometres from the town.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Now, Witness, do you remember the day that Srebrenica fell?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P106
utterances.text: Srebrenica fell on the 11th of July, 1995. That's when I set off from my home.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: What happened to your wife and other members of their family? Did they join you that day?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P106
utterances.text: We were told that Srebrenica, the safe area, enclave, had fallen, and women and old people went to Potocari, while the army and the others who felt they could get through the woods, we set off to get to Tuzla through the woods. With my family, I got to the village of Babuljice, and they set off towards Potocari, and I set off towards Jaglici. That's where we parted on the 11th of July, about 7.00 in the evening. I arrived at Jaglici about half past 9.00. That's where they said we would all meet up. That's where I spent the night. In the morning I set off from Jaglici, at about 20 to 1.00, exactly. That was the time. I didn't have the watch but I asked a colleague of mine what the time was. He told me it was 20 to 1.00. We were going direction of Buljim. We crossed the line. When we found ourselves beneath Buljim, there was a convoy that stopped. Somebody shouted from the woods: What's happening? What are you waiting for? And the column stopped. And then they went into the woods. They cursed a person who said that the convoy was lost. And I asked who was this, and somebody said this was Golic. I didn't know this person called Golic. And then he set off towards the person who said the convoy was lost. And I heard from the left-hand side of the hill, I heard somebody shouting: What are you waiting for? And he cursed. And there was shooting that started. People dispersed. Nobody was looking where they were going. I went down a brook. The brook was dry. There were people lying about. Whether they were dead, wounded, I don't know. I wasn't looking around. I went down there, found a stream, and going downstream, and there were 10 to 12 of us. We got to a neighbour, a neighbour who was married to someone from Kamenica. I asked him: Where are we going? Where are we? So we followed an asphalt road. They said left to this is Kamenica. So we started going along the left-hand side of the road alongside a wood. And we sat in that wood and darkness started to fall. And we could hear some noise beneath the hill. We then went in the direction of this noise. Darkness had fallen. After about 500 metres, we heard shooting. There was shooting from Praga. We didn't know who was shooting, where they were shooting towards. We then turned back. I didn't know what would happen. I then went into a kind of a valley. I could only be hit from the sky, because nobody could see me. And there was nobody around. I was trying to call around. Nobody was answering. There would be another machine-gun burst, and there would be people shouting, saying that wounded should be carried out. I started to go in the direction of the voice saying that wounded should be taken care of. Perhaps I went a hundred, 150 metres. I thought I would be killed in the wood. I said: Don't shoot. They asked me who I was. I said who I was. I said: Who are you? They said, I'm Suad. So I said, wait for me. I found the man. He said, Are you Suad. I said, I am. There was a man who was lying down, so I sat next to him. He said, do you have anything in your backpack. I said I did. He said, I didn't eat anything for two days. So I said if you haven't eaten, here it is, eat. So I gave him some food. And then we got up from there. There were so many dead around us, you could just step on the dead. I recognised one of them as being my neighbours. And I said to this Suad: Give me a lighter or a match, if you have, so I can recognise this person. So he did. So then I lost this man Suad. I never found him again. Wounded were being taken to a hill. There would be somebody shouting from the wood.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Witness, please allow the Prosecutor to ask you questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Witness, I would like just to ask you a couple of more questions about what you just told the Judges. Now you said that you left Jaglici on the 12th of July, just shortly before 1.00, I think you said.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P106
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: -- 1.00. Now, how many people --

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: How many people were around you in Jaglici?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P106
utterances.text: Well, no one counted. No one even thought of counting. But there must have been between 18 and 20,000. Towards the end, I left. Jaglici was somewhere behind me.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Were there people who had arms in that column?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P106
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Were you armed?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P106
utterances.text: No. I had my hunting rifle, which I gave to a relative of mine, in Jaglici. I left without my rifle. I never saw my rifle or my in-law after that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Can you tell us --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P106
utterances.text: Or my son-in-law after that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Can you tell us what you were wearing that day.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P106
utterances.text: I was wearing black trousers. I had a white sweater on and a shirt.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: So those were civilian clothes?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P106
utterances.text: Civilian clothes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: How about the other people who were around you? What were they wearing? Also civilian clothes?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P106
utterances.text: Most of them were wearing civilian clothes, because the soldiers were up front. I didn't see anyone from the command or from the municipality when I arrived in Jaglici.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Now, you described to us that on that day you were walking through the woods, 12th of July, there were two clashes, two times you described shooting. Can you tell the Judges who were shooting.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P106
utterances.text: We passed through their line where the first ambush was. That was where they held the lines. They had trenches, communicating trenches. No one opened fire on us. When we passed below Budini [phoen], we came across a road where this column had stopped and this is where the first ambush was. The Serbian aggressors must have opened fire. They opened fire from the hill. We were between the hills, in the woods.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Now, you said that you were carrying wounded up on the hill. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P106
utterances.text: Yes, I do. That was the second ambush.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: What did you do on the next day, on the 13th of July? Where were you then, in the morning?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P106
utterances.text: I was above Kamenica, on a hill. Kamenica Brdo. I didn't know that area at all. I only heard them mention the name Kamenica. On the 13th of July, it was a Thursday, we were there. There were quite a few people there, and that is where we were surrounded and captured. They told us to take our wounded with us. I was carrying Mujo Turkovic. His leg was broken above the knee. His brother had been wounded in the shoulder, and he asked me not to leave him behind, as we were descending. We crossed a river. He said: Put that wounded down.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Can you wait a second.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P106
utterances.text: There were two of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Witness, you just said that you surrendered. To whom did you surrender, and how did that occur?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P106
utterances.text: We surrendered to the Serbian aggressors when they surrounded us. They took -- they had towels or T-shirts attached to sticks and said: Don't shoot, we're surrendering. We descended down a field. It was a big field. I descended for 12 or 13 metres. I didn't want to be shot. Then there was crossfire from the other side. They were raising these sticks with the T-shirts attached to them and they shouted: Don't shoot. We're surrendering. And --

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Witness, you said they had white towels or white T-shirts. Who were they?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P106
utterances.text: These people of ours who were raising these sticks to which white towels and T-shirts had been attached, they were shouting: Don't shoot. We're surrendering.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Now, why did you surrender, you and your people who were around you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P106
utterances.text: Well, there was no other option for us. I wanted to flee again. There was an imam. I can say his name. He said: Don't be crazy. Don't try to run away. Can you see all these people here? I've remained there. I didn't try to run away. They forced us down towards the asphalt road. There were two soldiers of theirs down there. We left the wounded. They searched us to see whether we had weapons, grenade, a knife, and they wanted money. I had a hundred marks here. I took them out. I said I didn't have any more money. I put my hands behind my neck, crossed the road, went to a field. We were all sitting in rows.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Can I stop you just for a moment, Witness? You said that two people searched you. Who were these people? Can you describe them to the Judges, please.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P106
utterances.text: That happened later on when we had all gathered in the field. They brought a tanker and they sprayed us with water. It was very hot. The day was very hot. And then on the right-hand side, there was a tank, and there was an anti-aircraft machine-gun on the tank. And the person on the tank directed this gun at us twice. There was someone in civilian clothes in front of us. He said: Stop fooling around. He didn't shoot. I can't claim that he did.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Just one moment, Witness.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P106
utterances.text: He was just provoking us.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: You mentioned an asphalt road. Which asphalt road are you talking about? Can you tell us what villages --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P106
utterances.text: The one that connected Konjevic Polje, Bratunac, and Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And in what area were you surrendering? Do you remember a village in that area?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P106
utterances.text: Kamenica. Kamenica Brdo. That is where we surrendered. They forced us down towards the asphalt road. I heard from Ramiz Muskic that he knew this Bogic. He said we had been in Lolici, where we had been sitting.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Now, you said you were taken to a place, a field. Can you describe to us a little bit more in detail. I think you said that you have seen a tank there, and you described a commander. And can you tell us what this commander was wearing.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P106
utterances.text: The person who ordered the man to raise the anti-aircraft machine-gun in the air, not to shoot at us, he had a uniform. He was wearing a uniform. I didn't know him. And as we were sitting there, they then issued an order. I heard Madzarevic say -- that was the surname, Madzarevic, from Visnjica. One had -- one of them searched us. I left 600 marks and two necklaces that belonged to my daughter and ten ducats. So they took this away from me. One of them asked to have 50 marks, German marks, for cigarettes. They didn't want to leave minimum the marks for cigarettes. He said: You'll have cigarettes enough. And we remained sitting there in that field. They called this policeman who in peacetime worked in Vlasenica, and they said: There's Amir, the policeman.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Just one --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P106
utterances.text: One of them called out to him.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Witness, before we get to the policeman, you mentioned a moment ago Madzarevic from Vlasenica. Was he one of the persons who were guarding you, who was guarding you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P106
utterances.text: He was a soldier. There were several soldiers around us. But he had a yellow ponytail and they said that we should be searched. And they searched us in various orders. Some of them found money, gold, a watch.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Now, Witness, apart from the ponytail, how did he look like? What was the wearing? And why do you know that it was Madzarevic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P106
utterances.text: They called him by his surname, Madzarevic. They just said "Madzarevic searched him." And he had a yellow ponytail. I knew him by sight. But I don't know his first name. The man with the yellow ponytail was the only one I knew.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: So you recognised two people, the man with the ponytail and Madzarevic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P106
utterances.text: I didn't recognise Madzarevic, but I did recognise the surname. I knew that in Visnjica, you could come across people with this surname.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness. Was Madzarevic wearing civilian clothes or a uniform?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P106
utterances.text: He was in uniform.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And the person with the ponytail?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P106
utterances.text: He was also in uniform.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Now, how many people of yours were around you at that time on that meadow?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P106
utterances.text: I didn't count them, and the idea didn't even occur to me. I was thinking about my own fate. I heard someone who was a nurse in front of me, and the imam, I heard them whispering and saying that there were about 2.000 people. But I didn't count the number of people and the idea didn't even occur to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness. How many soldiers were guarding you? Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P106
utterances.text: There were quite a few of them. They didn't beat us. They didn't provoke us. They gave people cigarettes. They gave smokers cigarettes. I just recognised that policeman. Someone called him by his surname, not by his first name. They approached him, greeted them, then they went to the left into a house and stopped there. They spent some time there. I don't know how long they spent and I didn't have a watch. Three of them returned with him. He stood to the left of us. He called out the brother and said: Give me the jacket. The brother got up, took his jacket, and he said: Who is that? He said: He's my brother. His second brother turned and called out to the third brother. He said: Who is he? He said: It's my third brother. And he said: He should go too. Three of the soldiers went with the three brothers. And above the house where the wounded had been taken, that is the spot at which they disappeared without a trace.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Now, you just mentioned a policeman and told us what happened to the policeman and his brothers. Do you recall the name of this policeman?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P106
utterances.text: Amir Gabeljic.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Was he a Muslim or a Serb policeman?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P106
utterances.text: A Muslim.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Now, you mentioned that there was a house with wounded people. How many wounded people were there with you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P106
utterances.text: Well, there were quite a few wounded people. They had been taken to that house, and nothing is known about any of them. I didn't count them. I knew Mujo Turkovic. I knew Nusret. Nusret had only been wounded in the shoulder, and the other person, his leg had been broken above the knee.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness. Now, you said earlier that water was brought at one time. Do you recall somebody complaining that he did not get enough water?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P106
utterances.text: Children who were perhaps -- children who went to the eighth grade would bring water. One of our people was sitting in front of me, perhaps in the third row. A child, a child I knew from a neighbouring village, was carrying a 5-litre cannister of water. He got up, stretched out his hands. Some people would have -- would drink on two or three occasions. I hadn't drunk at all. A soldier kicked him in the head. A second soldier kicked him in the head. He started bleeding from the nose and the mouth. Someone took him by the collar and he was removed. They pulled him about 5 or 6 metres away from us, and he was -- a burst of fire was opened and he was shot. He remained in the field, and that young man saw the body when he arrived.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Now --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P106
utterances.text: And Mladic --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction. Mladic saw the body when he arrived.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Now, Witness, do you recall at any time seeing buses or trucks on that asphalt road?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P106
utterances.text: They were passing through from Potocari, with women, children, old men. There were lorries without tarpaulins and with tarpaulins, and there were buses too. And they more or less stopped and watched us sitting there in the field.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Did the buses continue?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P106
utterances.text: The buses continued towards Vlasenica and Kladanj.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Do you remember at what time in the afternoon, or whatever time you think you have seen the buses?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P106
utterances.text: I didn't have a watch. I tried to guide -- I tried to tell by the sun. It was about 2.00 or 3.00.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Now, did you see senior VRS officers coming to that field?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P106
utterances.text: I saw Mladic come. I recognised him. I watched him on television as soon as he arrived. I could see it was General Mladic. His first words were: Isn't it better for you to surrender than to die? Naser has left you. He's run away to Tuzla. It's not good to fight against the Serbs. Families have almost been evacuated. They're in Tuzla, Kladanj, Sevenice [phoen]. In two or three days, you'll probably be exchanged too. Everyone will return to their families. No one will beat you; no one will provoke you. We'll provide you with food. It's warm here. It's very hot for you here. We'll place you somewhere -- we'll find accommodation for you where it's cooler. There was an applause and we said thank you. I raised my hand. He said: What? I said: Can you see that I'm barefoot? I showed him my right foot. I have shoes in my rucksack. Can you take them? Can I put my shoes on? He said you'll get your shoes. I said thank you, General. He then left and about 15 or 20 minutes later the man in civilian clothes said we should form a column four by four. We started forming the column and we headed in the direction of Kravica. I didn't know this place. We went down the asphalt road, and on the right-hand side of the road there was an UNPROFOR vehicle. I don't know who was in it. There was no reaction. And on both sides --

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Before we go to Kravica, just one more question to you: Was there a time when the Serb soldiers asked for volunteers to come out?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P106
utterances.text: Yes. I forgot about that. They asked for about 13 -- 25 to 30 men. They climbed onto the lorry, threw down spades. I recognised a relative of mine. He climbed onto the lorry. The lorry started, and where they were taken, I don't know. They disappeared without a trace. I saw that they threw spades and pickaxes onto a lorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness. You said that somebody ordered you to form a column four by four. Was that the same person you had described earlier as the commander who directed his soldiers not to point the gun at --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P106
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Now --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P106
utterances.text: He was at the head of the column. He had a 53 or an 84. I don't know. I couldn't distinguish it. The person who ordered us to form a column with four men abreast, and the column headed in the direction of Kravica. When we arrived in Kravica, in front of that hall, that must have been some sort of agricultural warehouse. I didn't know that place. A bus was parked there in front of the warehouse. And we passed between the warehouse and the bus. There were two doors. I entered the second entrance.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Just one --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P106
utterances.text: I entered the hall through the second entrance.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Now, on the way between the field and Kravica, were there soldiers standing, guarding you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P106
utterances.text: On both sides of the column, every 6 or 7 metres there was a soldier, with automatic rifles, and they had belts across their chests. From the place where we were sitting, in the direction of Kravica, on both sides of the column.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Now, you said that when you arrived at the warehouse, that there was a bus. Now, on which side of the asphalt road was the warehouse?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P106
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: On which side? Was it left or right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P106
utterances.text: On the right-hand side of the road, from the direction we were coming from, that's where the warehouse was. And in front of the warehouse there was a bus that was parked there. Between the warehouse and the asphalt road.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Do you recall that there were houses in that area?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P106
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And where were the houses?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P106
utterances.text: There were houses both on the left and on the right-hand side of the asphalt road. The warehouse was the first building on the right-hand side, as far as I can remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Now I would like Your Honours, the witness to be shown Exhibit 10.1. You can have mine, and put it onto the ELMO, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Now, Witness, if you could have a look at this picture, and I believe you have seen it yesterday in my office. Can you tell us from which direction --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P106
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: -- you came when you were part of that column? Just have a look at it first, and then put it, please, back onto the ELMO, if you can do that.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P106
utterances.text: This is the asphalt road.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes. Can you please put it back and turn towards the ELMO, towards the machine which is on your right side. And now point it where you came from.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P106
utterances.text: I came from this direction. This is the side where the warehouse was. It was on this door that I entered.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And do you remember through which door the first part of the column entered?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P106
utterances.text: The first door.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Now if you could be given --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P106
utterances.text: Because when I got in to the warehouse, up to this door, it was all filled up. There was absolutely no room for anyone else. If you had dropped a lighter, it would have fallen on somebody. There was no free space at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Just one moment, Witness. If you could take a pen and mark with a cross the little door you've just shown us where you entered the warehouse.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P106
utterances.text: That's the first door. This is the second door. The second door that I entered through. This is where the bus was. Shall I also mark that? Between the warehouse and the --

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes, please. Yes. And perhaps you can make a circle around the cross where the bus was standing.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P106
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
